Nothing unusual about the bicycle. Here's a very rough estimate to how much I think everything cost back in 2012 when I built it.

  • Frame: ~$300
  • Fork: ~$75
  • Saddle: ~$110
  • Wheelset: ~$200
  • Fenders: ~$50
  • Gearset: ~$100
  • Saddlebag: ~$50
  • Lights and electronics: ~$80
  • Shifter levers: $50
  • Brakes system: ~$50
  • Rear rack: ~$30
  • Handlebars/stem: ~$50
  • Bicycle U-lock: ~$100 (a little overboard, yes)
  • Other things like the kickstand, water bottle holder, portable pump, repair tools in the saddle bag,

Then you can add on different bags and panniers, which add up. But this is my baby. It's how I get around the city.

Bonus bicycle picture. This is an old picture, I've since taken off the rear fold out basket, and flipped the stem to raise my handlebars a bit.

Thanks for the reply and explanation! I'm impressed that you built it! I'm still a little confused though. I don't know jack shit about bicycles-- what makes this superior/different from other bikes? Is it just crazy durable parts, or easy to pedal and perfectly balanced? I imagine it'd be easy for you to fix for sure, and I do see that it has lights and good storage. Just curious.

No problem, GoAskErin! :-)

Well, I can't tell you if it's really superior or not, but I've had very little problems with it in the three years/4500+miles I've had it.

I guess I'll start off with the frameset (frame and fork). It's a steel frame that uses Chromoly (Chrome Molybdenum) steel. CrMo steel is a lot lighter than older carbon steels from the 60s and 70s. It provides a nice ratio of weight to strength vs cost compared to other frame materials like aluminum, carbon fiber, and titanium. If I crash on my bicycle, I'm not worried about it's structural integrity (to a degree) as I would be if I had an aluminum or carbon fiber bicycle (even though those are lighter). Since I commute, I want something built like a tank. It takes bad road conditions like a champ.

What's crazy is that I have one of the cheaper CrMo steel frames.

The saddle is a Brooks saddle, which is super comfortable. I have spoiled my ass because of it.

The rest of the parts are all probably mid range parts, but they've lasted incredibly well. Mainly all I do for upkeep is oil the chain every few weeks, pump up the tubes every week, and clean it maybe once a year.

I find it easy to fix mainly because I built it xd

But for the record, my bicycle isn't nearly as expensive as the bicycles of some other enthusiasts or professionals.
